title: Reference ranges, explained: How lab tests are interpreted
summary: Learn what a reference range means, how to read a blood test, and why laboratory test [AL3.1]values may vary by person, test method, and updated guidance.
body_markdown:
When you get your lab results, you'll often see a "reference range" listed alongside your values. If your result falls outside that range, it can be easy to assume something is wrong. But reference ranges are more nuanced than many people realize.


Understanding what reference ranges are, what they mean, and why they can change over time can help you have more informed conversations with your healthcare provider.


## What are reference ranges?


A reference range is the range of results typically seen for a specific lab test. It helps your healthcare provider interpret your results and understand what they may mean for your health.


Different laboratory tests measure different substances in the body, such as cholesterol, blood sugar, hormones, or micronutrients like vitamin B12 and magnesium. For each test, a reference range is established using data from a large group of people who meet specific health criteria.


It's important to remember that a reference range is a tool for interpretation. It is not a strict definition of health or disease.


## What do reference ranges mean?


Reference ranges help healthcare providers determine whether a result is typical or whether further evaluation may be needed.


If your test result falls within the reference range, it is generally considered typical. But if the result falls outside the reference range, it does not necessarily mean something is wrong.


Many factors can influence test results, including age, sex, medical history, medications, diet, and other individual characteristics. Healthcare providers interpret laboratory results alongside symptoms, medical history, and other clinical information.


For this reason, reference ranges should be viewed as one piece of a larger clinical picture rather than a standalone diagnosis.


## Why do reference ranges change?


Science is constantly evolving. As researchers collect more data and gain a better understanding of health and disease, medical organizations may update recommendations and laboratories may reassess how test results are interpreted. In addition, reference ranges for the same test performed at different laboratories may vary, and new test technologies, processes, and methods may result in changes to a test’s reference range.


Vitamin D is a good example. Many labs once considered levels of 30 ng/mL or higher sufficient, but as research expanded our understanding of vitamin D's role across multiple body systems, some guidelines evolved to no longer recommend a specific target blood level for vitamin D.


Currently,[levels of 20 ng/mL or more are considered sufficient for most people](https://ods.od.nih.gov/factsheets/VitaminD-HealthProfessional/) , and the risk of deficiency increases at serum concentrations of less than 12 ng/mL. Most labs have adjusted their reference range to align with that guidance.


> "Reference ranges are based on the best available evidence at a given point in time," says Marcia Eisenberg, PhD, chief scientific officer and senior vice president at Labcorp. "As new research emerges, medical experts may update recommendations to ensure patients and providers make decisions based on the most current scientific understanding."


This change does not mean previous testing was incorrect. Rather, it reflects how medical guidance evolves when new evidence becomes available. As scientific understanding advances, recommendations may be refined to better reflect the latest research.


Reference ranges and clinical guidelines are designed to support informed healthcare decisions, and periodic updates are a normal part of evidence-based medicine. While recommendations may change over time, the goal remains the same: helping patients and healthcare providers make informed decisions based on the most current understanding of health, disease, and scientific evidence.
